osaka_tako_ume_honten_dotonbori.notes: [Oden · Dotonbori, since 1844] Calling itself the oldest oden shop in Japan, Tako Ume has simmered kanto-daki on Dotonbori since 1844, a counter of twelve around the oden pot and a window at the back onto the river. The broth takes its depth from saezuri, whale tongue, which the founder first used; order it, with the tako kanroni of sweet simmered octopus eaten with mustard, then daikon, potato, egg and the seasonal items, and a cup of sake warmed in tin. Writers from 織田作之助 to 開高健 ate here (official site). Budget ¥3,000–8,000 in 2026, plus a ¥275 appetiser; book by phone after 15:00. Open 16:00–21:50 daily.

roles: Fifth-generation owner (official site)
Founder: 岡田梅次郎 (official site)
chef_bio.background: Per the official site: an oden and sake house ("上燗屋") open since 1844 on Dotonbori, now in its fifth generation, from the founder 岡田梅次郎 to 岡田哲生, and called the oldest oden shop in Japan. The founder first used saezuri, whale tongue, which gives its kanto-daki a deep flavour; baleen-whale tongue is still bought and prepared in house, and the tako kanroni of madako has been simmered in the traditional broth since the start. Sake is warmed in tin tanpo in hot water and served in tin cups. Writers including 織田作之助, 池波正太郎, 檀一雄, 田辺聖子 and 吉田健一 were customers, and 開高健, a customer from the grandfather's day, wrote ten pages on Tako Ume in a novel. The current owner recalls an uncle, the previous owner, saying the shop lasted a hundred years because parents bring their children, who later bring theirs; that memory, on a hard winter night after the Lehman shock, set the aim of keeping the shop for the next hundred years.
chef_bio.philosophy: "Keep a place where parents bring their children, for the next hundred years" (official site, translated).

osaka_ramenza_yuto_nishinakajima.notes: [Ramen · Nishinakajima-Minamigata, Jiro-style niboshi bowls] A 20-seat ramen shop among the restaurants of Nishinakajima-Minamigata, open since 2021, serving Jiro-style bowls with a niboshi (dried sardine) or bonito broth: thick chewy noodles under a heap of bean sprouts and cabbage, back fat and grilled chashu, with noodle weight, vegetables, fat and sauce chosen when you hand over your ticket. Garlic is only added on request, and cayenne pepper on the table is the house twist. Bowls run about ¥1,000; the abura soba ends with rice and a raw egg in the bowl. One diner traced the bowl to a shop in Abeno Lucias that closed in January 2024 and found the same dish here (April 2024). osaka_konamon_mitsukuni_uranamba.notes: [Okonomiyaki · Ura Namba, okonomiyaki and creative monja with wine] Up a flight of stairs in Ura Namba, a calm Japanese room of sunken horigotatsu tables that bills itself as an "upmarket" okonomiyaki house and, as one diner found, is one of the few that take bookings. The head chef's okonomiyaki uses 100% Japanese wheat and a Kyoto-style bonito dashi and comes fluffy, loaded with shrimp and scallops; the yakisoba and modern-yaki use fresh noodles from the noodle works behind the shop, which several diners rate as the real star. The monjayaki go far from the classic, cooked for you at the table: basil Genovese, white miso with mochi, mapo, ebi-chili, bibimbap. Plenty of side dishes for drinking, all of the KENZO ESTATE wines and Japanese whisky. Tabelog Okonomiyaki 100 in 2025. Book ahead (walk-ins were turned away on a September 2026 night); open daily for lunch and dinner to 23:00.

A course runs from ¥15,000. Long a favourite for business dinners; expect ¥20,000–¥30,000 a head. Closed Sundays.

A favourite for birthdays and family celebrations; children are welcome in private rooms. Closed Mondays and the third Monday to Wednesday.

osaka_imai_kishou_ekimae_dai1.notes: [Japanese · Umeda, a seasonal counter under the station buildings] A quiet Japanese restaurant at the far western end of the Osaka Ekimae Dai-1 Building basement, where "Ofukuro no Aji Imai", which fed office workers here for over forty years, merged with "Shiki no Aji Kishou" of the Tenjinbashi-suji arcade, whose chef Sato had cooked Japanese food for fifteen years (Tabelog). The site says the menu has changed every single day since opening. Lunch is a bargain: ¥1,000 for a Saga wagyu beef bowl, an oyako-don or a marinated seafood bowl, each with a small seasonal side dish, salad and soup. At night sit at the counter for sashimi, beef-tendon stew, cream croquettes or dobin-mushi, or book a course from ¥4,400.
